idiom_name: service class registered in the built-in container + DbContext as unit of work
implementation_notes: The service is an ordinary class registered with AddScoped and constructor-injected into the controller or minimal-API endpoint. EF Core's DbContext supplies the unit of work: one SaveChangesAsync call is transactional by default, while Database.BeginTransactionAsync is needed when a use case must span several saves or coordinate multiple database operations. If the use case emits an integration event, add an outbox record before SaveChangesAsync and let a separate dispatcher publish it after commit; a publisher call cannot be made atomic with the database by awaiting it afterward.
pitfalls: Wrong move: publish an integration event after SaveChangesAsync; failure: the database is committed but the event is lost; instead: persist an outbox record before SaveChangesAsync and dispatch it after commit.
Registering the DbContext as a singleton, or sharing it across concurrent requests, corrupts the change tracker; keep it scoped.
A retrying execution strategy rejects manually started transactions unless the whole operation runs inside CreateExecutionStrategy().ExecuteAsync.

variants.name: One command handler per use case (MediatR)
variants.idiom_name: IRequestHandler<TCommand, TResult> dispatched by a mediator
variants.implementation_notes: Microsoft's microservice guidance packages the application layer as one command handler class per command, dispatched by a mediator so controllers only translate transport input; the handler is still the thin orchestrator (load, tell the model, save, publish) and all domain rules stay in the aggregates. Choose it when the one-to-one mapping between command and handler and the pipeline behaviours (validation, logging, transaction) matter more than seeing a single verb's dependency inventory in its constructor.
pitfalls: A handler per command multiplies classes; teams that dislike the file count should keep one service class per noun - the orchestration is identical.
Pipeline behaviours must not smuggle domain rules into the application layer; they are for cross-cutting concerns only.
The mediator hides the dependency set of the use case, so the constructor-inventory advantage of the plain service class is lost.
